title: The development and application of the emotional dimensions of a soundscape
research_question: To understand and define the emotional dimensions of a soundscape, and to explore how the resultant dimensional space could have a practical application in decision making.

participants.description: Experiment 1: 22 jurors (age range 22-70, mean 38, 19 males, 6 females, normal hearing). Experiment 2A: 9 jurors. Experiment 2B: 9 different jurors. All recruited from the University of Warwick.
participants.recruitment: Email advertisement at the University of Warwick

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Experiment 1: 8 urban soundscape recordings (e.g., busy traffic, human sounds, urban parks with distant traffic and wildlife, café atmosphere, crowds). Experiment 2: 8 binaural soundscape recordings from University of Warwick campus (roads with traffic, human sounds, green spaces with distant traffic, wildlife, water features). Application section: 13 soundscape recordings, including 6 common urban soundscapes (market square, park, street) and 7 modified market square recordings with added sounds (ACU, water fountain, birds, church bell, human rowdiness, near traffic).

measures.instrument: 1-9 semantic differential rating scales for 5 dimensions: 'Calmness and Relaxation', 'Comfort and Reassurance', 'Vibrancy and Arousal', 'Informative', 'Intrusiveness and Sense of Self'
Intelligibility (%), Sound Pressure Level (dBA), Loudness (Sones), Sharpness (Acum), Roughness (Asper), Fluctuation Strength (Vacil) calculated with B&K's Sound Quality software.

findings.antecedent: Urban soundscapes (rated on 5 semantic differential scales)
findings.consequent: Two independent emotional dimensions of soundscape perception
findings.mechanism: Principal Component Analysis decomposes semantic descriptors into underlying dimensions.
findings.quote: These two components retain orthogonality and together, explain 80% of the variability in the original 5 dimensions.

findings.antecedent: Urban soundscapes with visual stimuli (rated on 5 semantic differential scales)
findings.consequent: Two independent emotional dimensions of soundscape perception
findings.mechanism: Principal Component Analysis decomposes semantic descriptors into underlying dimensions.
findings.quote: These two components retain orthogonality and explain 76% of the variability in the original 5 dimensions.

findings.antecedent: Urban soundscapes without visual stimuli (rated on 5 semantic differential scales)
findings.consequent: Two independent emotional dimensions of soundscape perception
findings.mechanism: Principal Component Analysis decomposes semantic descriptors into underlying dimensions.
findings.quote: These two components retain orthogonality and explain 73% of the variability in the original 5 dimensions.

findings.antecedent: Presence vs. absence of visual stimuli accompanying urban soundscapes
findings.consequent: The two principal emotional dimensions (Calmness, Vibrancy) of soundscape perception
findings.mechanism: The underlying emotional dimensions of soundscape perception are robust across visual context.
findings.quote: From the results of the Principal Component Analyses presented in Table 2, we can see that an urban soundscape can be characterized by 2 principal dimensions

findings.antecedent: Different urban soundscapes (e.g., busy street, park with birdsong, market square, coffee shop, shopping centre, street with traffic murmur/people)
findings.mechanism: Different soundscapes evoke different emotional responses, leading to distinct positions in the 2D perceptual space.
findings.quote: It shows for instance, that from hearing the soundscape, this particular listener rated a busy street as not calming, but fairly vibrant, whereas a park with birdsong was rated highly calming, but not so vibrant.

findings.antecedent: Design interventions (e.g., adding church bells, rowdiness, near traffic, ACU filter, birds, water fountain) to a market square soundscape
findings.consequent: Perceived calmness and vibrancy of the soundscape
findings.mechanism: Design interventions modify the soundscape, which in turn alters emotional perception.
findings.quote: adding new things into the soundscape reduced the feeling of calmness. Church bells, rowdiness and nearby traffic were all shown to increase the feeling of vibrancy within the space, whereas air-conditioning units, birdsong and a water fountain all decreased the feeling of vibrancy.

findings.antecedent: Adding church bells, rowdiness, or near traffic to a market square soundscape
findings.mechanism: These sound elements contribute to a less calm emotional response.
findings.quote: adding new things into the soundscape reduced the feeling of calmness.

findings.antecedent: Adding church bells, rowdiness, or near traffic to a market square soundscape
findings.mechanism: These sound elements contribute to a more vibrant emotional response.
findings.quote: Church bells, rowdiness and nearby traffic were all shown to increase the feeling of vibrancy within the space

findings.antecedent: Adding air-conditioning units (ACU), birdsong, or a water fountain to a market square soundscape
findings.mechanism: These sound elements contribute to a less vibrant emotional response.
findings.quote: whereas air-conditioning units, birdsong and a water fountain all decreased the feeling of vibrancy.

findings.mechanism: Objective acoustic measures like dBA are insufficient to capture the subjective emotional perception of soundscapes.
findings.quote: many of the recordings have roughly the same level, but they are perceived very differently for calmness and vibrancy. This is important as it serves as evidence that simply using objective measures is not sufficient to fully understand listener perception of the soundscape.

mechanisms: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) as a method to decompose semantic descriptors of soundscapes into underlying emotional dimensions.
The emotional dimensions of 'Calmness' and 'Vibrancy' provide a perceptual space to map and compare soundscapes based on how they make people feel.
moderators: Visual context (presence/absence of images with soundscapes)
implementation_implications: Planners and decision makers can use the 2-D perceptual space to position existing and future soundscapes, understand how design interventions (e.g., water features, traffic flow changes) move soundscapes within this space, and facilitate target-setting for soundscape design.
The framework can be used to present how different frequencies of air conditioning might change perception of a place.
The framework can illustrate potential effects of larger design interventions (e.g., introducing water features, changing road layouts).
The framework can demonstrate how social and technological changes (e.g., hybrid/electric vehicles) might alter calmness and vibrancy perception.
The emotional dimensions can help protect and preserve sound environments in quiet areas or places of cultural identity by showing how increased noise could change perception.

tables.description: Starting set of 5 emotional dimensions and their semantic descriptors used in the experiments.
Component Score Coefficient Matrices (Varimax Rotation) for Experiment 1, 2A, and 2B, showing loadings of 5 semantic dimensions on 2 principal components and variance explained.
Sample of 13 soundscape recordings used for exploring applications of the calmness-vibrancy perceptual space, including objective psychoacoustic parameters.

limitations: Demographic issues require data from large populations to understand nuances between groups for soundscape perception.
Listening state ('tuned in'/'tuned out') and intended user activities affect soundscape perception and need to be considered in design.
Quantitative acoustic measurements (e.g., dBA) often disconnect from subjective emotional responses, highlighting the need for subjective measures.
More evidence is needed to understand how specific design interventions will position soundscapes within the perceptual space.
Challenges of context, personal experience, cognition, and subjectivity in assessing soundscapes make the task considerable.
